pathway_rules: Oral bioavailability is the product of three fractions, F = Fa x Fg x Fh: the fractions absorbed across the enterocyte membrane, escaping gut-wall metabolism, and escaping hepatic first-pass extraction. Being a product rather than a tally of hazards, an unfavourable finding at one step is not on its own evidence for the negative class.

P-gp (ABCB1) and BCRP (ABCG2) are co-localized, saturable efflux pumps on the apical enterocyte membrane with overlapping substrate specificity, returning substrates to the gut lumen. Efflux lowers the absorbed fraction only where it can compete with passive influx: at ordinary oral doses the pumps saturate, and a highly permeable compound is bypassed faster than they cycle.

Efflux substrate status is thus evidence for the negative class only together with low passive permeability - high polar surface area, high hydrogen-bond count, or ionization across the intestinal pH range. The efflux-metabolism alliance, in which P-gp cycling prolongs enterocyte residence and raises CYP3A4 exposure, likewise needs low permeability and unsaturated gut-wall metabolism.

CYP3A4 is the dominant oxidative enzyme of gut wall and liver, but CYP engagement becomes evidence for the negative class only where intrinsic clearance approaches a high hepatic extraction ratio, whose correlates are high lipophilicity with a sterically unhindered, metabolically soft oxidation site and no polar group limiting hepatic uptake.

CYP2D6 is absent from the intestinal wall and so cannot reduce the absorbed fraction, acting only on hepatic first pass; at a few percent of hepatic P450 content it is rarely the dominant clearance route. Its pharmacophore - a lipophilic base of pKa ~8-10 with the oxidation site ~5-7 A from a planar aromatic ring - describes a well-absorbed chemotype.

Small heteroaromatic scaffolds (pyridine, pyrimidine, imidazole ring systems) with MW < 400 Da, LogP 1-3 and TPSA < 75 A^2: low desolvation energy and favorable passive transcellular diffusion across the intestinal membrane.
N-methylation or aromatic fluorine substitution: lowers the hydrogen-bond-donor count and metabolic susceptibility, increasing membrane permeability and passive transcellular absorption.
Very high lipophilicity (LogP > 5 with TPSA < 50 A^2): strong partitioning into the lipid bilayer supports adequate passive absorption through lipophilic membrane permeation alone.
Lipinski Rule-of-Five-compliant scaffold (MW < 500 Da, LogP <= 5, HBD <= 5, HBA <= 10): a physicochemical profile associated with a high prior probability of oral absorption.
no_features: High TPSA (> 120-140 A^2): a large polar surface area imposes a high desolvation penalty and poor passive membrane permeability across the intestinal epithelium.
More than 5 hydrogen-bond donors: excessive aqueous solvation opposes partitioning into the membrane and limits passive transcellular absorption of the molecule.
Large MW (> 600-700 Da), especially combined with many rotatable bonds: high molecular size and flexibility give poor passive diffusion regardless of lipophilicity.
Multiple carboxylic-acid groups: extensive ionization at intestinal pH leaves little neutral fraction and opposes partitioning into the membrane for passive absorption.
Permanently charged centers (e.g. quaternary ammonium): no neutral species exists at any pH, precluding passive transcellular absorption across the intestinal membrane.
